extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, actors, and literary critics (aspiring and practicing writers/performers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing and judging heroic/epic poetry (and related performative elements): narration, moral purpose, characterisation, imagery, structure, language, and appropriate imitation. Also includes related advice on stagecraft and clarity of diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of Divinity and Poetry in Narration
rubrics_metrics.description: If Milton's Poem flags any where, it is in this Narration, where in some places the Author has been so attentive to his Divinity, that he has neglected his Poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not allow theological or didactic preoccupation to overwhelm poetic craft; maintain poetic qualities (imagery, rhythm, ornament) even when handling sacred/divine subject matter. Example: some episodes succeed where the subject admits poetical ornaments (Babel, Plagues of Egypt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ poetical ornaments where subject allows
rubrics_metrics.description: The Narration... rises very happily on several Occasions, where the Subject is capable of Poetical Ornaments, as particularly in the Confusion which he describes among the Builders of Babel, and in his short Sketch of the Plagues of Egypt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use elevated imagery and ornamentation selectively—apply them in episodes naturally suited to poetical decoration to heighten effect without excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of scriptural allusion and elevated images
rubrics_metrics.description: The River-Dragon is an Allusion to the Crocodile... This Allusion is taken from that Sublime Passage in Ezekiel... Milton has given us another very noble and poetical Image in the same Description, which is copied almost Word for Word out of the History of Moses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate and lofty allusions (e.g., to scripture) can enrich imagery; imitations may be effective when elevated and integrated into original poetic context. Beware of mere borrowing without elevation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episode focus aligned with principal design
rubrics_metrics.description: As the principal Design of this Episode was to give Adam an Idea of the Holy Person, who was to reinstate human Nature... the Poet confines himself to the Line of Abraham, from whence the Messiah was to Descend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep episodes tightly focused on the work's overarching purpose; choosing the proper genealogical or thematic line (e.g., Abraham/line of promise) gives liveliness and unity to digressive visions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic ending: leave reader in tranquillity and satisfaction
rubrics_metrics.description: An Heroick Poem, according to the Opinion of the best Criticks, ought to end happily, and leave the Mind of the Reader, after having conducted it through many Doubts and Fears, Sorrows and Disquietudes, in a State of Tranquility and Satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the conclusion restores moral or emotional balance; even after tragic events, provide closure that reharmonizes the reader (Milton supplies this by making Satan mortified and the first parents comforted with visions/promises).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral unity / deducible principal moral
rubrics_metrics.description: I do not scruple to say... no just Heroick Poem ever was or can be made, from whence one great Moral may not be deduced. That which reigns in Milton... That Obedience to the Will of God makes Men happy, and that Disobedience makes them miserable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An epic should support an overarching moral or ethical principle that naturally emerges from the fable and episodes; the principal moral functions as the soul of the fable while many under-morals may be drawn from particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrastive character representation for moral effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Satan is represented miserable in the height of his Triumphs, and Adam triumphant in the height of Misery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray characters contrastively to illuminate moral outcomes—e.g., depict adversary's humiliation alongside protagonists' consolation to reinforce the poem's moral and emotional resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varieties of poetic beauty (sublime, soft, natural)
rubrics_metrics.description: I have endeavoured to shew how some Passages are beautiful by being Sublime, others by being Soft, others by being Natural; which of them are recommended by the Passion, which by the Moral, which by the Sentiment, and which by the Expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and cultivate different modes of beauty—match treatment (passion, moral, sentiment, expression) to the kind of beauty desired in a passage; analyze why a passage works (source of beauty) to replicate effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius expressed by invention, allusion, imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: I have likewise endeavoured to shew how the Genius of the Poet shines by a happy Invention, a distant Allusion, or a judicious Imitation; how he has copied or improved Homer or Virgil, and raised his own Imaginations by the Use which he has made of several Poetical Passages in Scripture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original genius combines fresh invention with well-chosen allusion and measured imitation of masters; imitation should be judicious—used to improve or raise one's own imagination rather than to slavishly copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural division should aid regular disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The Number of Books... This second Division was made with great Judgment... It was not done for the sake of such a Chimerical Beauty as that of resembling Virgil in this particular, but for the more just and regular Disposition of this great Work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize books/parts for clarity and regularity of the whole action; structural choices should serve the work's internal needs, not mere imitation of other poets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclude with vivid, image-rich speeches for consolation
rubrics_metrics.description: The last Speeches of Adam and the Arch-Angel are full of Moral and Instructive Sentiments... the last beautiful Speech which is ascribed to the Mother of Mankind, without a secret Pleasure and Satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concluding speeches to encapsulate moral instruction and to provide readerly consolation—rich imagery and instructive sentiments heighten the final emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of natural, relatable scene-details to evoke tears
rubrics_metrics.description: The Scene which our first Parents are surprized with, upon their looking back on Paradise, wonderfully strikes the Reader's Imagination, as nothing can be more natural than the Tears they shed on that Occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In major moments, employ small natural details (tears, gestures) to make emotional reactions credible and to move the reader; realism in feeling aids sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid concluding lines that revive anguish unnecessarily
rubrics_metrics.description: These two Verses, though they have their Beauty, fall very much below the foregoing Passage, and renew in the Mind of the Reader that Anguish which was pretty well laid by that Consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful that final lines do not undermine the consolatory effect of the ending by reintroducing earlier anguish; choose concluding phrasing that sustains the intended emotional closure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage and theatre as moral/amending influence
rubrics_metrics.description: It is, with me, a Matter of the highest Consideration what Parts are well or ill performed, what Passions or Sentiments are indulged or cultivated, and consequently what Manners and Customs are transfused from the Stage to the World, which reciprocally imitate each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theatre practitioners should be conscious of social impact—well-regulated stagecraft portraying vices and virtues can reform manners; avoid performances that encourage immoral imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate casting and fidelity of role
rubrics_metrics.description: If I were to speak of Merit neglected, mis-applied, or misunderstood... when thus I celebrate Wilks, I talk to all the World who are engaged in any of those Circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign actors to roles matching their capacities; faithful, apt portrayal (tenderness, contrition, comic effect) produces social exemplars and educates audiences about character types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gesture, motion and dance as essential expressive tools
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be a great Improvement... if Dancing were more regarded, and taught to all the Actors... Such elegant Entertainments as these, would polish the Town into Judgment in their Gratifications; and Delicacy in Pleasure is the first step People of Condition take in Reformation from Vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train actors in gesture, motion and dance to render subtle emotional and social nuances; physical expression refines performance and influences audience taste and manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comic/character roles to expose vices
rubrics_metrics.description: When we come to Characters directly Comical, it is not to be imagin'd what Effect a well-regulated Stage would have upon Men's Manners. The Craft of an Usurer, the Absurdity of a rich Fool... might be for ever put out of Countenance by proper Parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-executed comic portrayals can shame or curb social follies—use satire and comedy to correct manners rather than merely to amuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid abuse of words; tie words to clear ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The first and most palpable Abuse of Words, he says, is, when they are used without clear and distinct Ideas... The Result of our Contemplations and Reasonings, while we have no precise Ideas fixed to our Words, must needs be very confused and absurd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In moral and literary discourse, ensure each significant word maps to a clear idea; avoid vague or loose terminology that produces confusion. Prefer definitions where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of word application
rubrics_metrics.description: The second [abuse] when we are so inconstant and unsteady in the Application of them, that we sometimes use them to signify one Idea, sometimes another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use key terms consistently; do not let a word denote different ideas across the same discourse, especially in moral writing, to avoid confusion and absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use definitions in moral discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid this Inconvenience... he earnestly recommends the use of Definitions. A Definition, says he, is the only way whereby the precise Meaning of Moral Words can be known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When discussing moral concepts, supply definitions to fix meanings—this supports clearer argumentation and avoids equivocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict Modesty and Assurance as distinct, balanced traits
rubrics_metrics.description: If I was put to define Modesty, I would call it The Reflection of an Ingenuous Mind... I take Assurance to be the Faculty of possessing a Man's self, or of saying and doing indifferent things without any Uneasiness or Emotion in the Mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating characters or prescribing behaviour, distinguish modesty (self-reflection, blush, inward sense of censure) from assurance (self-possession, composed action). Encourage cultivation of both: modesty guards honour; assurance guards composure and moral steadiness.
